display_name: Shafer Vineyards One Point Five, Napa Valley
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Stag’s Leap vineyard sits at 600 ft on the volcanic shoulder of the Mayacamas, where iron-rich Hambright soils force Cabernet to dig through fractured tuff for water; Shafer bottles that stress as One Point Five, a cassis-packed 15.3 % ABV red that drinks like hillside Napa at half the price of Hillside Select.",
  2022": "A warm, even season gave small berries with 26 °Brix at pick; the resulting wine is denser than 2019 but keeps Shafer’s trademark bay-leaf lift. Expect blackcurrant, dark chocolate, and a graphite edge that will unfurl for 15–20 years.",
  "terroir_expression": "Volcanic Hambright gravel shot through with tuff and compressed ash limits vigorous valley-floor loam; vines yield 2.2 tons/acre versus 4+ on the floor. That berry concentration translates into smaller, thicker-skinned fruit, so One Point Five carries 15 g/L tannin at harvest—almost double valley averages—yet the gravel drains fast, keeping acidity bright (pH 3.65) and preventing the cooked compote character you sometimes taste in lower-elevation Napa Cab.",
  "vinification_summary": "Hand-harvested at night, 48 h cold soak at 8 °C to extract color without seed tannin, then native ferment in 1-ton open-tops; free-run wine ages 20 months in 40 % new French oak (Taransaud, Sylvain) and the balance once-used barrels so oak never tops 50 %—a restraint level that lets the hillside cassis and graphite speak.",
  "food_food": "Nashville hot chicken—the wine’s 15.3 % alcohol and mountain tannin and black-fruit weight tame capsaicin while the bay-leaf note echoes the spice blend. Dry-aged rib-eye with porcini butter—grilled fat softens the 70 % new-oak tannin, umami doubles the wine’s savory streak. Peking duck pancakes—hoisin sweetness pulls out dark-plum fruit, high alcohol cuts through rendered skin. Aged white cheddar—protein binds tannin, salt amplifies cassis. For fine dining: squab breast, black-cherry reduction; the bird’s iron tang mirrors the volcanic soil blood-like note.",
  "comparable_wines": "Dunn Napa Valley Cabernet — similar hillside Mayacamas sourcing, iron-laced cassis but even more tannic and half the oak. Heitz Napa Valley — valley-floor opposite, softer tannins, more mint; shows what elevation does. Pine Ridge Stags Leap District — contiguous AVA, same volcanic soils, slightly plusher texture but parallel graphite spine.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry Cabernet with mountain tannins and volcanic graphite drive",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink 2026–2038; 55 °F, 70 % RH, lie bottles horizontal; the 2022’s extra phenolics buy it an extra 3–4 years over valley-floor Napa Cabs.",
  "value_assessment": "$127–140 positions One Point Five between $90 Stags Leap Artemis and $200+ hillside Cabernets; you get Shafer’s pedigree and 20-month élevage for the cost of entry-level Stags Leap District bottlings. Comparable quality exists at $110 (Pine Ridge) but not with Shafer’s track record; buy on release—retailers rarely discount it.",
  "market_position": "Restaurant by-the-glass programs in steak-centric chains (Del Frisco’s, Fleming’s) list it at $28–32 because the name recognition moves inventory; private collectors in Texas and Florida cellar 3–6 bottles as their “upstairs” Napa without crossing the $200 line; it’s the introductory handshake before people graduate to Hillside Select.",
  "insider_take": "Skip it if you want elegant Bordeaux restraint—this is 15 % ABV mountain fruit wrapped in 40 % new French oak. What you’re paying for is consistency: Shafer has produced One Point Five every vintage since 2005, and the ’22 carries the same Hambright signature as the ’08, proving hillside Stags Leap can ripen without going jammy.",
